en.note:
The idea

English has two present forms (I work, he works). Dutch has three forms, so it's only a little harder. The Dutch present also covers "I'm working" and often the near future: Ik werk morgen = I'm working tomorrow. There is no separate "-ing" form.

How to conjugate in three steps

1. Find the stem: drop -en from the infinitive. werken → werk.
2. With ik use the bare stem.
3. With jij, u, hij, zij (she), het add -t. In the plural (wij, jullie, zij) use the full infinitive.

werken (to work)wonen (to live)
ikwerkwoon
jij / uwerktwoont
hij / zij / hetwerktwoont
wij / jullie / zijwerkenwonen

Spelling rules

The sound never changes: only the spelling does, to keep the same sound when the word gets shorter.

  • Long vowel: in wo-nen the o is long but written single, because the syllable ends in a vowel. When you drop -en the syllable closes, and to keep the long sound you have to double the vowel: woon. Likewise maken → maak, lopen → loop.
  • Double consonant: zitten → zit, liggen → lig. Dutch never writes two identical consonants at the end of a word.
  • v → f and z → s at the end of a word: leven → leef, lezen → lees.
  • If the stem already ends in -t, don't add another t: zitten → hij zit. If it ends in -d, add the t anyway, even though you can't hear it: vinden → hij vindt.

Questions with jij/je

Dutch has no helper "do": to ask a question you simply put the verb first (unit 7). When jij/je follows the verb, the -t drops: Jij werkt but Werk je? This applies only to jij/je: Werkt hij? Werkt u? keep the t.

The most common irregular verbs

zijn (to be)hebben (to have)gaan (to go)doen (to do)
ikbenhebgadoe
jij / ubenthebtgaatdoet
hij / zijisheeftgaatdoet
wij / jullie / zijzijnhebbengaandoen

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Translating "I'm working" word for word: ik ben werken → just ik werk.
  • Using doen like the English helper "do": Doe je spreken Nederlands? → Spreek je Nederlands?
  • Keeping the t in the question: Werkt je? → Werk je?
  • Writing a single vowel: ik wom, ik mak → ik woon, ik maak.
en.vlaams: With gij/ge the verb keeps its -t even in questions: "Werkt ge vandaag?". The verb zijn becomes "ge zijt". You'll hear it everywhere in Flanders, but you don't need to use it yourself.
